blocks.text: **The problem.** Given a sorted array of **distinct** integers `nums` and a `target`, return the index of `target` if it's there. If not, return the index where it **would be inserted** to keep the array sorted. Your algorithm must run in **O(log n)** time.

blocks.alt: The sorted array 1, 3, 5, 6. Target 5 is at index 2. Target 2 belongs between 1 and 3, at index 1. Target 7 goes after everything, at index 4. Target 0 goes before everything, at index 0. In every case the answer is the first index whose value is at least the target.

elements.text: the answer is always the first index with nums[i] >= target

blocks.text: The idea: where binary search gives up

Found or not, the answer is the **first index whose value is at least the target** — the lower bound. You can find it with the lower-bound template, but there's a neat fact about the classic loop too: when it ends without finding the target, `low` has stopped **exactly at the insert position**. Every value left of `low` is smaller than the target and every value right of `high` is bigger, and the loop ends with `low = high + 1`, so `low` is the first index past all the smaller values.
2. Classic binary search, then return low

blocks.caption: When the target isn't found, watch where low stops: it's the insert position.

blocks.text: **Time O(log n), space O(1).** The only change from Binary Search is the last line: `return low` instead of `return -1`.
**Time O(log n), space O(1).** In an interview, mention the library call, then write the loop yourself.

blocks.alt: Linear scan: O(n) time, O(1) space. Classic loop, return low: O(log n) time, O(1) space. Lower bound: O(log n) time, O(1) space.

items: **Target bigger than everything** — the answer is `nums.length`, an index past the end.
**Target between two values** — it goes at the index of the bigger one.
**Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array** — lower bound and upper bound together (Pattern 2).
**Insert Interval** — find where a new interval goes in a sorted list of intervals, then merge.
**Longest Increasing Subsequence (O(n log n))** — for each value, binary search its insert position in a list of tails.
